PhGPO: Pheromone-Guided Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon Tool Planning

Yu Li    Guangfeng Cai    Shengtian Yang    Han Luo    Shuo Han    Xu He    Dong Li    Lei Feng ††thanks: Corresponding author.
Abstract

Recent advancements in Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in executing complex tasks through tool use. However, long-horizon multi-step tool planning is challenging, because the exploration space suffers from a combinatorial explosion. In this scenario, even when a correct tool-use path is found, it is usually considered an immediate reward for current training, which would not provide any reusable information for subsequent training. In this paper, we argue that historically successful trajectories contain reusable tool-transition patterns, which can be leveraged throughout the whole training process. Inspired by ant colony optimization where historically successful paths can be reflected by the pheromone, we propose Pheromone-Guided Policy Optimization (PhGPO), which learns a trajectory-based transition pattern (i.e., pheromone) from historical trajectories and then uses the learned pheromone to guide policy optimization. This learned pheromone provides explicit and reusable guidance that steers policy optimization toward historically successful tool transitions, thereby improving long-horizon tool planning. Comprehensive experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed PhGPO.

Introduction

Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in executing complex tasks through tool use (Zhang et al. 2025; Luo et al. 2025; Schick et al. 2023; Yang et al. 2025b). By invoking external tools such as web search (Zhou et al. 2024), computer operation (Qiu et al. 2025b), and code execution (Yang et al. 2025a), agents can access up-to-date information and take actions beyond static parametric knowledge. As the tool space expands, many real-world tasks require a tool-use trajectory, where early choices constrain later reachable states and determine whether the entire trajectory succeeds (Yao et al. 2022; Liu et al. 2025). When tool-use trajectories extend to ten to twenty steps, as in Toolathlon (Li et al. 2025b), long-horizon tool planning becomes difficult: agents must choose from hundreds of tools, yet even when a successful trajectory is discovered, its transition patterns are hard to explicitly store and reliably reuse, which hinders effective learning in such a large tool space (Xu et al. 2025; He et al. 2025).

Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a natural way to leverage interaction experiences and feedback to update the policy for long-horizon tool planning (Yu et al. 2025; Li et al. 2025c; Hou et al. 2025). However, interaction experiences are typically absorbed implicitly into the policy parameters, leaving no explicit record of historically successful tool transitions. As a result, even after a successful tool-use trajectory is discovered, its transition patterns remain implicit in the policy parameters and cannot be directly reused as guiding information. When successful trajectories are rare, the exploration of RL becomes inefficient because the agent must search again for similar long-horizon trajectories (Lu et al. 2025; Li et al. 2025a).

In this paper, we argue that an explicit transition prior can be distilled from historically successful trajectories, which would be helpful to policy optimization. We validate our viewpoint with a two-stage pilot experiment (Figure 1): Firstly, we collect verified successful tool-use trajectories and distill their transition patterns into an explicit transition prior. Secondly, we use this prior to reweight the policy’s next-tool distribution in accord with verified transitions. As shown in Figure 1, the explicit transition prior improves both sample efficiency and final success, with larger gains as trajectory length increases.

Motivated by the above analysis, we would like to seek an explicit transition prior that can be learned from historical trajectories and reused during policy optimization. To realize such a prior, we draw inspiration from Ant Colony Optimization (ACO), where the pheromone summarizes historically successful paths and encourages them to be taken again (Dorigo et al. 1996; Chari et al. 2025). Based on this inspiration, we propose Pheromone-Guided Policy Optimization (PhGPO), which learns an explicit transition prior from historical trajectories, and this transition prior acts as the pheromone in ACO. Concretely, PhGPO organizes tools into a tool-transition graph based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) (Luo et al. 2025) and associates each transition with a pheromone value. During policy optimization, we integrate the pheromone values into next-step tool selection, making historically successful tool transitions more likely to be reproduced. It is noteworthy that the pheromone is reinforced by verified successful tool-use trajectories and decays over time, which keeps the transition pattern reusable and up to date. We further construct a set of frequent argument invocations for each tool, enabling the agents to learn not only which tool to call but also how to invoke it effectively.

Based on the pheromone mechanism as described above, our PhGPO adopts a progressive training pipeline to equip an agent with long-horizon tool planning abilities. Firstly, PhGPO begins with supervised warm-up using a next-tool prediction objective to provide a stable initialization. Secondly, PhGPO performs pheromone-guided reinforcement learning with a progressive schedule: it injects the correct next tool with a decaying probability and progressively cedes control to the policy, which enables pheromone to be continually updated from accumulated policy-driven successes. As the accumulated pheromone becomes more reliable, it fully leverages pheromone guidance for trajectory generation to optimize long-horizon performance. We empirically evaluate PhGPO on three long-horizon tool-planning benchmarks, including Toolathlon (Li et al. 2025b), TOUCAN (Xu et al. 2025) and TRAJECT-Bench (He et al. 2025), which cover diverse real-world tool-use scenarios with long multi-step tool-use trajectories. Across these benchmarks, PhGPO consistently produces tool-use trajectories that more closely match the reference trajectories on complex tasks, demonstrating that pheromone enables effective reuse of historical successes and improves long-horizon tool planning performance.

Our main contributions can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    Explicit reuse in long-horizon tool planning. We show that transition patterns in successful tool-use trajectories are typically absorbed implicitly into the policy parameters, making them hard to reuse and slowing learning when verified successes are rare.

  • •

    PhGPO with pheromone as an explicit transition prior. We propose PhGPO, which distills successful trajectories into an explicit transition prior working as pheromone, and uses it to guide policy optimization toward historically successful tool transitions.

  • •

    MCP-grounded graph and progressive training. We build an MCP-grounded tool-transition graph to maintain pheromone and introduce a progressive training pipeline to accumulate and exploit it over long tool-use trajectories, achieving consistent gains on Toolathlon, TOUCAN, and TRAJECT-Bench.

Related Work

Retrieval-augmented tool use. Tool selection at scale is a central challenge for tool-using agents, and many methods use retrieval to narrow the candidate set by fetching relevant documentation, schemas, or demonstrations (Yao et al. 2022; Shinn et al. 2023; Min et al. 2025b; Min et al. 2025a). Early prompting-based agents interleave reasoning and action selection over retrieved evidence (Yao et al. 2022; Shinn et al. 2023). More recent systems further train retrievers or tightly couple retrieval with tool-calling models to improve robustness under large and evolving tool pools (Patil et al. 2024; Schick et al. 2023; Qin et al. 2023; Guo et al. 2024; Li et al. 2023), and dedicated benchmarks and pipelines increasingly treat tool selection as an information retrieval problem (Chen et al. 2024; Braunschweiler et al. 2025; Wang et al. 2025a; Pan et al. 2025). While retrieval strengthens per-step grounding, long-horizon tool-use trajectories still depend on correct multi-step transition patterns learned across decisions.

Graph-structured tool planning and search. Beyond retrieval, many methods exploit explicit structure among tools by organizing APIs and dependencies into graphs or trees, and then planning through graph traversal, heuristic search, or learned graph representations (Liu et al. 2024a; Liu et al. 2024b; Jiang et al. 2025; Chen et al. 2025b; Zhuang et al. 2024). Some approaches search or expand over tool graphs to produce multi-step tool-use trajectories (Liu et al. 2024a; Liu et al. 2024b; Jiang et al. 2025), while others generate executable tool graphs or DAG-like plans (Chen et al. 2025b). Robustness to evolving tool interfaces can also be improved through interactive search and self-updating mechanisms (Chen et al. 2025a). While structured representations can reduce the effective search space, these methods typically rely on heuristics or supervised planning signals and do not maintain an explicit, adaptive transition prior distilled from accumulated successes to guide policy optimization.

Reinforcement learning for tool use. Reinforcement learning methods have been increasingly used to improve multi-step tool use under sparse outcomes (Yu et al. 2025; Li et al. 2025c). Recent work studies tool-integrated optimization with verifiable or execution-based rewards (Wei et al. 2025b), and explores hierarchical agent designs that separate high-level planning from tool execution (Zhang 2025). Related settings also investigate agents that interleave language with executable code and learn tool-use strategies from outcomes (Feng et al. 2025b; Dong et al. 2025). Despite these advances, successful experience is still often absorbed implicitly into the policy parameters, which can slow learning in long-horizon settings when verified successful trajectories are rare.

Experience reuse and agent memory. Explicit experience reuse has been studied through storing and replaying successful behaviors rather than relying solely on implicit parameter updates (Tang et al. 2025; Wang et al. 2025b). Record-and-replay paradigms cache trajectories or routines to accelerate future problem solving (Qiu et al. 2025a; Feng et al. 2025a). However, these approaches rarely maintain structured transition statistics distilled from accumulated successes as an explicit transition prior, especially for long-horizon tool-use trajectories on large tool-transition graphs.

Methodology

In this section, we present Pheromone-Guided Policy Optimization (PhGPO) for long-horizon tool planning. PhGPO is built around a simple principle: long-horizon tool use should explicitly accumulate and reuse historically successful tool transitions from verified tool-use trajectories. Inspired by Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) (Dorigo et al. 1996), PhGPO instantiates the explicit transition prior as pheromone on a tool-transition graph. Pheromone is reinforced by verified successful trajectories and decays over time, yielding an adaptive supervision signal that can be incorporated into next-step tool selection for policy optimization. In this way, PhGPO converts trajectory-level success into transition-level pheromone on the graph, which steers policy optimization toward historically successful tool transitions while avoiding stale bias through decay.

Tool-Transition Graph from MCP

The goal of long-horizon tool use is to first select the next tool and then specify an executable invocation. To this end, we build a tool-transition graph from MCP that captures tool transitions from verified trajectories and explicitly represents tools and their transitions, providing a structured space for modeling multi-step tool-use trajectories and their transition patterns. We also construct a set of frequent argument invocations for each tool, which captures how tool arguments are frequently invoked.

Tool-transition graph. Let 𝒱Tool={v1,…,vN}\mathcal{V}_{\text{Tool}}=\{v_{1},\dots,v_{N}\} be the base tools exposed by MCP. We view a tool-use trajectory as a path over 𝒱Tool\mathcal{V}_{\text{Tool}} and define a directed edge (vi,vj)∈ℰ(v_{i},v_{j})\in\mathcal{E} when vjv_{j} follows viv_{i} in a trajectory. This graph captures tool-to-tool dependencies and provides the substrate for accumulating transition experience on edges.

Argument-invocation set. The invocation of each tool vi∈𝒱Toolv_{i}\in\mathcal{V}_{\text{Tool}} also depends on the specific structure of tool arguments. For each tool vi∈𝒱Toolv_{i}\in\mathcal{V}_{\text{Tool}}, we construct a set of frequent executable argument invocations 𝒱Arg\mathcal{V}_{\text{Arg}} that captures how tool arguments are frequently invoked, denoted by 𝒱Arg​(vi)={vi(1),…,vi(Ki)}\mathcal{V}_{\text{Arg}}(v_{i})=\{v_{i}^{(1)},\dots,v_{i}^{(K_{i})}\} where vi(j)v_{i}^{(j)} denotes the jj-th argument-invocation pattern among KiK_{i} key patterns of the tool viv_{i}. To make the mapping explicit, we define tool-to-invocation association edges ℰarg=⋃i=1N{(vi,vi(k))∣vi(k)∈𝒱Arg}\mathcal{E}_{\text{arg}}=\bigcup_{i=1}^{N}\{(v_{i},v_{i}^{(k)})\mid v_{i}^{(k)}\in\mathcal{V}_{\text{Arg}}\}. An edge (vi,vi(k))∈ℰarg(v_{i},v_{i}^{(k)})\in\mathcal{E}_{\text{arg}} indicates that vi(k)v_{i}^{(k)} is an argument-invocation associated with tool viv_{i}.

Based on both the tool-transition graph and the argument-invocation set, we can have a factorized decision at step tt: the agent first selects the next tool at∈𝒱Toola_{t}\in\mathcal{V}_{\text{Tool}}, then selects an argument invocation ut∈𝒱Arg​(at)u_{t}\in\mathcal{V}_{\text{Arg}}(a_{t}) to instantiate an executable invocation template.

Pheromone as an Explicit Transition Prior

Our PhGPO integrates both task-agnostic pheromones with task-dependent pheromones from verified successful tool-use trajectories.

Task-agnostic pheromones. We maintain two task-agnostic pheromones, including τToolagn​(vi,vj)\tau^{\text{agn}}_{\text{Tool}}(v_{i},v_{j}) extracted from the tool-transition graph 𝒱Tool\mathcal{V}_{\text{Tool}} and τArgagn​(vi,vi(k))\tau^{\text{agn}}_{\text{Arg}}(v_{i},v_{i}^{(k)}) extracted from the argument-invocation set 𝒱Arg\mathcal{V}_{\text{Arg}} respectively. After executing a trajectory ξ\xi, we compute a quality score q⁡(ξ)∈[0,1]q(\xi)\in[0,1], in terms of the match ratio to the reference tool-use trajectory. For each traversed tool and each selected argument invocation in ξ\xi, we apply ACO-style deposition and evaporation:

τagn←clip⁡((1−ρ)​τagn+α​q​(ξ),[τmin,τmax]).\displaystyle\tau^{\text{agn}}\leftarrow\mathrm{clip}\bigl((1-\rho)\tau^{\text{agn}}+\alpha\,q(\xi),~[\tau_{\min},\tau_{\max}]\bigr). (1)

Here, ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) is the evaporation rate that denotes the decayed degree of outdated statistics, α>0\alpha>0 is the deposition rate, and q⁡(ξ)q(\xi) scales the reinforcement for transitions in the tool-use trajectory ξ\xi, with higher-quality tool-use trajectories contributing more to the pheromone updates. We clip pheromones to [τmin,τmax][\tau_{\min},\tau_{\max}] to make better utilization of pheromones and limit excessive concentration on a small subset of tools. It is noteworthy that the construction of both τToolagn\tau^{\text{agn}}_{\text{Tool}} and τArgagn\tau^{\text{agn}}_{\text{Arg}} follows the same way as shown in Eq. (1).

Task-dependent pheromones. For each transition (vi,vj)(v_{i},v_{j}), we maintain an edge memory bank ℳi​j\mathcal{M}_{ij} that stores tuples (𝒆,q)(\bm{e},q), where 𝒆\bm{e} is a task embedding and qq is the quality score of a verified successful tool-use trajectory that includes this transition. Given a task description xx, we compute 𝒆x=ϕ⁡(x)\bm{e}_{x}=\phi(x) using a sentence encoder ϕ\phi and retrieve memories whose cosine similarity exceeds a threshold:

ℳi​j(x)={(𝒆,q)∈ℳi​j∣sim(𝒆x,𝒆)≥θsim,∀𝒆}.\mathcal{M}_{ij}(x)=\{(\bm{e},q)\in\mathcal{M}_{ij}\mid\mathrm{sim}(\bm{e}_{x},\bm{e})\geq\theta_{\text{sim}},\forall\bm{e}\}. (2)

Then, we estimate task-dependent pheromone by similarity-weighted averaging:

τdep​(vi,vj∣x)\displaystyle\tau^{\text{dep}}(v_{i},v_{j}\mid x) =τ0+∑(𝒆,q)∈ℳi​j​(x)sim⁡(𝒆x,𝒆)​q∑(𝒆,q)∈ℳi​j​(x)sim⁡(𝒆x,𝒆)+ϵ\displaystyle=\tau_{0}+\frac{\sum_{(\bm{e},q)\in\mathcal{M}_{ij}(x)}\mathrm{sim}(\bm{e}_{x},\bm{e})\,q}{\sum_{(\bm{e},q)\in\mathcal{M}_{ij}(x)}\mathrm{sim}(\bm{e}_{x},\bm{e})+\epsilon}
⋅(τmax−τ0),\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\cdot(\tau_{\max}-\tau_{0}), (3)

where τ0\tau_{0} is a base value, ϵ\epsilon is a small constant for numerical stability, and the scaling (τmax−τ0)(\tau_{\max}-\tau_{0}) keeps τdep\tau^{\text{dep}} in a comparable range. It is noteworthy that the construction of both τTooldep​(vi,vj∣x)\tau^{\text{dep}}_{\text{Tool}}(v_{i},v_{j}\mid x) and τArgdep​(vi,vi(k)∣x)\tau^{\text{dep}}_{\text{Arg}}(v_{i},v_{i}^{(k)}\mid x) follows the same way as shown in Eq. (3).

Nevertheless, as shown in Eq. (3), if the edge memory bank ℳi​j\mathcal{M}_{ij} contains very few memories (𝒆,q)(\bm{e},q), the estimated task-dependent pheromone could be unreliable. Therefore, we need to assign a corresponding confidence ci​j​(x)∈[0,1]c_{ij}(x)\in[0,1] to each task-dependent pheromone for representing their reliability:

ci​j​(x)=min⁡(1,nact/nmin)⋅smax⋅q¯,\displaystyle c_{ij}(x)=\min(1,n_{\text{act}}/n_{\min})\cdot s_{\max}\cdot\bar{q}, (4)

where nactn_{\text{act}} is the number of memories in ℳi​j\mathcal{M}_{ij}, nminn_{\min} is a pre-defined minimum number of elements in ℳi​j\mathcal{M}_{ij}, smaxs_{\max} is the maximum similarity observed, and q¯\bar{q} is the mean quality score of the retrieved memories. In this way, the final pheromone can be fused by simultaneously considering task-agnostic pheromones and task-dependent pheromones:

τTool​(vi,vj∣x)\displaystyle\tau_{\text{Tool}}(v_{i},v_{j}\mid x) =(1−w⋅ci​j​(x))⋅τToolagn​(vi,vj)\displaystyle=(1-w\cdot c_{ij}(x))\cdot\tau^{\text{agn}}_{\text{Tool}}(v_{i},v_{j})
+w⋅ci​j(x)⋅τTooldep(vi,vj∣x),\displaystyle\quad+w\cdot c_{ij}(x)\cdot\tau^{\text{dep}}_{\text{Tool}}(v_{i},v_{j}\mid x), (5)

where ww controls the maximum contribution of task dependence. We apply the same fusion way as shown in Eq. (5) for calculating τArg\tau_{\text{Arg}}.

Pheromone-Guided Policy Optimization Training

Learning long-horizon tool planning from scratch is difficult because early training lacks reliable successes to build an explicit transition prior. We adopt a progressive pipeline that stabilizes basic behavior, gradually accumulates pheromone from verified tool-use trajectories, and then performs pheromone-guided policy optimization.

Supervised warm-up. We first pre-train the policy with a next-tool prediction objective:

ℒSL=−log⁡πθ​(at∗∣st),\mathcal{L}^{\text{SL}}=-\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}^{*}\mid s_{t}), (6)

where at∗a_{t}^{*} is the reference next tool. This stage ignores pheromone guidance and moves the policy away from random tool selection. By establishing tool-selection capabilities, the model can generate plausible initial tool-use trajectories that facilitate future success.

Pheromone as guidance. Building on this initialization, we introduce a pheromone-guided exploration strategy to navigate long-horizon tool-ues task completion. Specifically, we incorporate pheromone as an explicit transition prior during trajectory generation, increasing the likelihood of collecting informative tool-use trajectories for policy learning. This pheromone-guided trajectory generation aligns well with group-based policy optimization (Anschel et al. 2025; Feng et al. 2025c), where learning signals depend on the quality of multiple rollouts per prompt. We adopt Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al. 2024) as the optimization backbone, since GRPO computes relative advantages within a rollout group. In long-horizon tool planning with a large tool space, unguided sampling can yield groups dominated by uniformly low-quality trajectories, weakening the relative learning signal. Pheromone-guided sampling increases the likelihood that each group contains higher-potential trajectories and meaningful contrasts, enabling GRPO to better leverage its group-based advantage to update the policy. We now present the sampling rule used for pheromone-guided sampling and the objective used to update the policy.

Pheromone-guided sampling. At each step tt, the policy network generates πθ​(at∣st)\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t}) given the current state sts_{t}. To incorporate historical experience, we integrate the policy with pheromone as an explicit transition prior. Specifically, we first select the top-KK candidates from πθ\pi_{\theta} as the sampling support, and then sample the next tool according to the pheromone-guided policy:

p⁡(at∣st,at−1)∝exp⁡(CLOSE\displaystyle p(a_{t}\mid s_{t},a_{t-1})\propto\exp\bigl( log⁡πθ​(at∣st)\displaystyle\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})
OPEN+β​log⁡τTool​(at−1,at∣x)),\displaystyle+\beta\log\tau_{\text{Tool}}(a_{t-1},a_{t}\mid x)\bigr), (7)

Once the base tool ata_{t} is selected, the agent selects an argument invocation ut∈𝒱Arg​(at)u_{t}\in\mathcal{V}_{\text{Arg}}(a_{t}) according to τArg​(at,ut∣x)\tau_{\text{Arg}}(a_{t},u_{t}\mid x). This argument choice is not parameterized by πθ\pi_{\theta} and is not updated during policy optimization. Here (at,ut)(a_{t},u_{t}) follows the tool-to-invocation association defined in Sec. Tool-Transition Graph from MCP.

Policy optimization. For each training instance, we sample MM tool-use trajectories using the pheromone-guided distribution in Eq. (7), obtaining returns {Rm}m=1M\{R_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M}. We compute group-relative advantages:

Am=Rm−R¯σR+ϵ,where​R¯=1M​∑m=1MRm,\displaystyle A_{m}=\frac{R_{m}-\bar{R}}{\sigma_{R}+\epsilon},\qquad\ \text{where}\ \bar{R}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}R_{m}, (8)

where ϵ\epsilon is a small constant for numerical stability. The policy πθ\pi_{\theta} is updated by minimizing the following objective:

ℒPG=−𝔼⁡[min⁡(rt​(θ)​Am,clip​(rt​(θ),1−ε,1+ε)​Am)],\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{\text{PG}}=-\mathbb{E}\left[\min\left(r_{t}(\theta)A_{m},\,\text{clip}(r_{t}(\theta),1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)A_{m}\right)\right],

where rt​(θ)=πθ​(at∣st)/πθold​(at∣st)r_{t}(\theta)=\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})/\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_{t}\mid s_{t}) denotes the probability ratio at step tt, and ε\varepsilon is the clipping threshold.

Progressive pheromone updates. Having introduced pheromone-guided sampling and the policy optimization objective, we apply them through a progressive training schedule that blends supervision and exploration to accumulate pheromone as an explicit transition prior. We introduce a learning curriculum over horizon lengths, starting from short horizons and gradually increasing to longer ones, and employ an oracle probability ptfp_{\text{tf}} decaying over time. Specifically, at each step tt, the action ata_{t} is determined as:

at={at∗,with prob. ​ptf,sampled from Eq. (7),with prob. ​1−ptf,a_{t}=\begin{cases}a_{t}^{*},&\text{with prob. }p_{\text{tf}},\\ \text{sampled from Eq.~\eqref{eq:sampling}},&\text{with prob. }1-p_{\text{tf}},\end{cases} (9)

where at∗a_{t}^{*} is the reference action. This keeps rollouts close to reference trajectories in the early phase, increasing the chance of collecting verified successful tool-use trajectories for pheromone updates in longer horizons. We employ a mixed objective that shifts from imitation learning to policy optimization:

ℒmixed=λ​ℒSL+(1−λ)​ℒPG−γ​ℋ​[πθ],\mathcal{L}^{\text{mixed}}=\lambda\mathcal{L}^{\text{SL}}+(1-\lambda)\mathcal{L}^{\text{PG}}-\gamma\mathcal{H}[\pi_{\theta}], (10)

where λ\lambda is annealed downwards and ℋ⁡[πθ]\mathcal{H}[\pi_{\theta}] denotes the entropy of πθ\pi_{\theta}. Accordingly, the explicit transition prior (pheromone) is updated from partially autonomous verified successful trajectories, making it increasingly reflect policy-selected transitions, instead of being dominated by purely teacher-forced ones. We concurrently increase the pheromone-controlling hyperparameter β\beta in Eq. (7) and the task-dependence weight ww in Eq. (5) as the number of accumulated trajectories grows, turning the initial pheromone values into a reliable transition signal.

Full-pheromone rollouts. As ptfp_{\text{tf}} decays and λ\lambda is annealed downwards, training transitions to fully autonomous rollouts with full pheromone influence:

π~​(a∣st)∝exp⁡(log⁡πθ​(a∣st)+βmax​log⁡τat−1,a),\tilde{\pi}(a\mid s_{t})\propto\exp\bigl(\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s_{t})+\beta_{\text{max}}\log\tau_{a_{t-1},a}\bigr), (11)

where βmax\beta_{\text{max}} is the maximum pheromone influence scheduled to be reached, and τat−1,a\tau_{a_{t-1},a} is a shorthand for the fused tool-transition pheromone τTool​(at−1,at∣x)\tau_{\text{Tool}}(a_{t-1},a_{t}\mid x). Similarly, argument-invocation utu_{t} is selected using the same pheromone-guided rule with τArg​(at,ut∣x)\tau_{\text{Arg}}(a_{t},u_{t}\mid x). The updated pheromone serves as an explicit transition prior during trajectory generation, encouraging the policy to reproduce historically successful transitions and argument invocations. Policy optimization is performed on tool-use trajectories collected under pheromone guidance. In parallel, pheromone updates follow the deposition and evaporation rule defined in Eq. (1), where evaporation reduces the influence of outdated statistics over time.

Collectively, training begins with supervised warm-up that provides a stable initialization for next-tool selection. It then proceeds with pheromone-guided reinforcement learning that uses pheromone as an explicit transition prior during trajectory generation and optimizes the policy with GRPO on tool-use trajectories collected under pheromone guidance. The training schedule gradually reduces oracle guidance via the decayed ptfp_{\text{tf}} and anneals λ\lambda downward, and the horizon curriculum increases task difficulty from short to long. This progression supports progressive pheromone accumulation from partially guided verified successes and later enables fully pheromone-guided trajectory generation for complex long-horizon tool-use trajectories.

Experiments

Experiment Setup

Dataset. We conduct experiments on three long-horizon tool-use benchmarks: Toolathlon (Li et al. 2025b), a benchmark built on MCP servers with hundreds of tools across diverse domains; TRAJECT-Bench (He et al. 2025), grounded in executable production-style APIs; and TOUCAN (Xu et al. 2025), a large-scale tool-agent dataset synthesized from MCP environments. Each instance is converted into an episode containing a task description, a reference tool-use trajectory, and the corresponding execution outputs. We filter episodes with verified successful trajectories and map each recorded tool call to our action representation by separating the base tool from its argument invocation. We construct fixed-seed training, validation, and test splits and report results on the test set.

Comparing Methods. We compare with a diverse set of representative tool-use baselines. Standard Prompting and Planning methods include the reasoning-action interleaving ReAct (Yao et al. 2022) and global-oriented Plan-and-Solve (Wang et al. 2023), alongside the Beyond-ReAct (Wei et al. 2025a) planner-executor architecture. Retrieval-Augmented Selection baselines comprise Gorilla (Patil et al. 2024), ToolReAGt (Braunschweiler et al. 2025), and the GCN-based Tool Graph Retriever (Gao et al. 2025). RL-based Optimization baselines consist of search-driven TreeRL (Hou et al. 2025), outcome-oriented ToRL (Li et al. 2025c), and process-level StepTool (Yu et al. 2025). Finally, Graph-based Frameworks include GAP (Wu et al. 2025) as well as GTool (Chen et al. 2025b), NaviAgent (Jiang et al. 2025), and ToolNet (Liu et al. 2024a), which leverage explicit tool-dependency structures for navigation or representation learning. All experiments are conducted using Qwen2.5-7B (Yang et al. 2024) and Llama3.1-8B (Grattafiori et al. 2024) as backbones. All baselines operate in the same tool-and-invocation decision space and share the same execution interface.

Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate performance using two metrics: (1) Match Ratio (M∈[0,1]M\in[0,1]), a trajectory-level measure quantifying the similarity between generated tool-use trajectories and reference trajectories in tool identity and ordering; and (2) Next-tool Accuracy (A∈[0,1]A\in[0,1]), a step-level metric measuring the correctness of the immediate next-tool selection.

Implementation Details. We fine-tune the backbones using LoRA (Hu et al. 2022) (r=64,α=128r=64,\alpha=128) to adapt the policy for long-horizon tool planning. Each state consists of the task description and a fixed-length truncated history of recent tool interactions. For decoding, we employ temperature (0.7), top-KK sampling (K=20K=20), and ϵ\epsilon-greedy exploration (ϵ=0.05\epsilon=0.05). The pheromone influence β\beta is linearly scheduled to a maximum of 0.8. We set the maximum trajectory length to 20 and sample M=5M=5 rollouts for optimization. Complete experimental details are in Appendix B.

Experimental Results

Overall performance compared with prior methods. Table 1 shows that PhGPO achieves the best performance on Toolathlon, TRAJECT-Bench, and TOUCAN under both Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3.1-8B. Compared with the strongest baselines across categories, PhGPO improves both Match Ratio and Next-tool Accuracy consistently, suggesting that the improvements are not limited to a single evaluation setting. The improvements appear on benchmarks with different task compositions and tool-use patterns, which indicates that the method generalizes across long-horizon tool-use scenarios. The fact that PhGPO maintains the lead under both backbones also suggests that the performance improvements are not driven by specific backbone.

Compared with prompting and retrieval-augmented baselines. Prompting and planning baselines remain substantially below learning-based methods, reflecting that long-horizon tool use requires sustained multi-step tool transitions that are difficult to maintain through in-context reasoning alone. These strategies can produce locally reasonable steps, but they lack an explicit mechanism to preserve transition consistency across a long sequence, making them susceptible to compounding errors. RAG methods often improve Next-tool Accuracy by narrowing plausible choices at each step, yet their Match Ratio remains limited on long-horizon episodes. This suggests that locally relevant retrieval does not reliably translate into globally consistent tool-use trajectories, because later tool transitions must remain compatible with earlier decisions, intermediate states, and previously chosen arguments as the horizon grows.

Compared with graph-based and RL-based optimization baselines. Graph-based navigation models consistently improve over prompting baselines and often achieve competitive Next-tool Accuracy, indicating that explicit structural constraints can regularize tool selection. RL-based optimization methods further improve long-horizon performance by learning from execution outcomes, with TreeRL as the strongest baseline overall. PhGPO advances beyond these approaches by incorporating pheromone as an explicit transition prior during rollout generation and policy optimization. In particular, this prior biases sampling toward tool-transition edges and argument invocation patterns that recur in verified successful trajectories, which reduces cascading errors from early missteps and improves multi-step consistency over long horizons. As a result, the agent more reliably maintains globally consistent tool-use trajectories that align with the reference.

Ablation Studies

We conduct ablation studies on Qwen2.5-7B using the same Toolathlon split, training budget, and evaluation protocol as the main experiment. All variants share the same backbone, optimizer, and policy optimization hyperparameters, and we only modify the specified component. We evaluate the full model and five ablated variants: (1) w/o Pheromone sets β=0\beta{=}0 throughout training; (2) w/o Mixed Curriculum removes the Mixed Curriculum phase that uses oracle guidance to progressively shape early rollouts. This variant still uses pheromones, and pheromone statistics are accumulated only from fully policy-driven rollouts; (3) Static Prior freezes the pheromone after the progressive training pipeline and disables subsequent updates; (4) w/o Evaporation sets ρ=0\rho{=}0 during fully pheromone-guided rollouts so pheromones only accumulate; and (5) w/o Task-dependent Pheromones disables task-dependent pheromones and fusion, using task-agnostic pheromones.

Table 2 shows that every component contributes to long-horizon alignment with the reference tool-use trajectories. The largest drop comes from removing the Mixed Curriculum phase, indicating that early oracle-guided rollouts help accumulate more reliable pheromone statistics before training becomes fully policy driven. Disabling pheromone guidance (β=0\beta{=}0) produces the second-largest degradation, with a larger drop in Next-tool Accuracy than in Match Ratio, suggesting that the explicit transition prior mainly improves stepwise tool-transition choices, which then compounds over long horizons into better trajectory-level alignment. Disabling task-dependent pheromones also degrades performance, indicating that retrieval helps activate task-matched transition evidence for the current instance. Finally, freezing pheromones after the Mixed Curriculum phase or disabling evaporation underperforms the full method, supporting the need for online updates and decay to keep the explicit transition prior aligned with the evolving policy distribution.

Visualization of transition structure

To qualitatively examine the transition structure learned by PhGPO, we present a representative long-horizon task involving sequential web retrieval and file manipulation. Figure 3 visualizes the evolution of the pheromone transition matrix between tools over training, together with the growth of pheromone values along a reference trajectory.

At the beginning of training, the heatmap is diffuse, indicating that pheromone values stay close to initialization and no transition pattern is strongly emphasized. As training proceeds (Epochs 8 and 16), pheromone concentrates on a small subset of transitions. Notably, transitions along the reference tool-use trajectory (WebSearch →\to FetchHTML →\to WriteFile →\to ReadFile →\to RunCmd) receive repeated reinforcement from verified successful trajectories, while many off-trajectory transitions fade as evaporation reduces the influence of older or less supported statistics. By Epoch 25, these reference transitions become clearly highlighted, illustrating how PhGPO accumulates and reuses validated transition patterns over training.

Conclusion

We proposed PhGPO, a pheromone-guided policy optimization framework that enables explicit reuse of verified successful tool-use trajectories for long-horizon tool planning. PhGPO maintains a pheromone-based explicit transition prior over tool-transition edges and argument invocation, updates it through deposition and evaporation, and incorporates it into rollout sampling to promote historically successful tool transitions over time. Experiments on long-horizon tool-use benchmarks, including Toolathlon, TRAJECT-Bench, and TOUCAN, show that PhGPO consistently improves Match Ratio and Next-tool Accuracy. These results support the role of pheromone as an explicit transition prior for long-horizon tool planning.

Appendix A A: Theoretical Motivation of Pheromone-guided Sampling

This appendix provides a principled view of the pheromone-guided sampling distribution in Eq. (7). The key idea is that the sampling rule can be derived as the closed-form solution of an entropy-regularized consensus problem that combines the neural policy with an explicit transition prior induced by pheromone.

Setup

At decision step tt, the policy produces a distribution πθ​(a∣st)\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s_{t}) over tools. Following Sec. Pheromone-Guided Policy Optimization Training, we restrict sampling to a finite support 𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t} constructed from the Top-KK candidates under πθ(⋅∣st)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t}). We use pheromone as an explicit transition prior through the fused tool-transition pheromone τTool​(at−1,a∣x)\tau_{\text{Tool}}(a_{t-1},a\mid x) defined in Sec. Pheromone as an Explicit Transition Prior, which already incorporates task-agnostic and task-dependent evidence via Eq. (5). To ensure log⁡τTool\log\tau_{\text{Tool}} is well-defined, we clip pheromone values:

τ¯​(at−1,a∣x)=clip⁡(τTool​(at−1,a∣x),[τmin,τmax]),τmin>0.\bar{\tau}(a_{t-1},a\mid x)=\mathrm{clip}\bigl(\tau_{\text{Tool}}(a_{t-1},a\mid x),[\tau_{\min},\tau_{\max}]\bigr),\qquad\tau_{\min}>0. (12)

We define the pheromone-induced explicit transition prior over the candidate set as

pτ​(a∣at−1,x)∝[τ¯​(at−1,a∣x)]β,a∈𝒜t,p_{\tau}(a\mid a_{t-1},x)\propto\bigl[\bar{\tau}(a_{t-1},a\mid x)\bigr]^{\beta},\qquad a\in\mathcal{A}_{t}, (13)

where β≥0\beta\geq 0 controls the strength of the explicit transition prior. The pheromone-guided sampling distribution used in our rollouts is

π~​(a∣st,at−1,x)∝exp⁡(log⁡πθ​(a∣st)+β​log⁡τ¯​(at−1,a∣x)),a∈𝒜t,\tilde{\pi}(a\mid s_{t},a_{t-1},x)\propto\exp\!\Big(\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s_{t})+\beta\log\bar{\tau}(a_{t-1},a\mid x)\Big),\qquad a\in\mathcal{A}_{t}, (14)

which is equivalent to the multiplicative form π~∝πθ(⋅∣st)pτ(⋅∣at−1,x)\tilde{\pi}\propto\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t})\,p_{\tau}(\cdot\mid a_{t-1},x) on the support 𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t}.

Entropy-regularized consensus objective

We derive π~\tilde{\pi} by solving for a distribution qq over the candidate set 𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t} that agrees with both the neural policy and the explicit transition prior, while retaining entropy:

maxq⁡𝔼a∼q​[log⁡πθ​(a∣st)+β​log⁡τ¯​(at−1,a∣x)]+η​ℋ​(q),s.t. ​∑a∈𝒜tq⁡(a)=1,q⁡(a)≥0,\max_{q}\;\mathbb{E}_{a\sim q}\!\Big[\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s_{t})+\beta\log\bar{\tau}(a_{t-1},a\mid x)\Big]+\eta\,\mathcal{H}(q),\quad\text{s.t. }\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{t}}q(a)=1,\;q(a)\geq 0, (15)

where ℋ(q)=−∑a∈𝒜tq(a)logq(a)\mathcal{H}(q)=-\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{t}}q(a)\log q(a) is Shannon entropy and η>0\eta>0 is an entropy weight.

Closed-form solution via Lagrange multipliers

Introduce a Lagrange multiplier γ\gamma for the normalization constraint and write the Lagrangian

ℒ⁡(q,γ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(q,\gamma) =∑a∈𝒜tq(a)(logπθ(a∣st)+βlogτ¯(at−1,a∣x))+η(−∑a∈𝒜tq(a)logq(a))+γ(∑a∈𝒜tq(a)−1).\displaystyle=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{t}}q(a)\Big(\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s_{t})+\beta\log\bar{\tau}(a_{t-1},a\mid x)\Big)+\eta\Big(-\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{t}}q(a)\log q(a)\Big)+\gamma\Big(\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{t}}q(a)-1\Big). (16)

Taking partial derivatives with respect to q⁡(a)q(a) and setting them to zero gives

log⁡πθ​(a∣st)+β​log⁡τ¯​(at−1,a∣x)−η⁡(1+log⁡q⁡(a))+γ=0.\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s_{t})+\beta\log\bar{\tau}(a_{t-1},a\mid x)-\eta\bigl(1+\log q(a)\bigr)+\gamma=0. (17)

Rearranging yields

log⁡q⁡(a)=1η​(log⁡πθ​(a∣st)+β​log​τ¯​(at−1,a∣x))+γη−1,\log q(a)=\frac{1}{\eta}\Big(\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s_{t})+\beta\log\bar{\tau}(a_{t-1},a\mid x)\Big)+\frac{\gamma}{\eta}-1, (18)

which implies the optimal solution

q∗​(a)∝exp⁡(1η​[log⁡πθ​(a∣st)+β​log⁡τ¯​(at−1,a∣x)]),a∈𝒜t.q^{*}(a)\propto\exp\!\Big(\tfrac{1}{\eta}\big[\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s_{t})+\beta\log\bar{\tau}(a_{t-1},a\mid x)\big]\Big),\qquad a\in\mathcal{A}_{t}. (19)

Setting η=1\eta=1 recovers Eq. (14), which matches our implementation in Eq. (7).

Equivalent KL projection view

The same objective admits an information-geometric interpretation. Let

r⁡(a)∝exp⁡(log⁡πθ​(a∣st)+β​log⁡τ¯​(at−1,a∣x)),a∈𝒜t.r(a)\propto\exp\!\Big(\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s_{t})+\beta\log\bar{\tau}(a_{t-1},a\mid x)\Big),\qquad a\in\mathcal{A}_{t}. (20)

Expanding KL(q∥r)=∑a∈𝒜tq(a)logq⁡(a)r⁡(a)\mathrm{KL}(q\|r)=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{t}}q(a)\log\frac{q(a)}{r(a)} gives

−KL(q∥r)=𝔼a∼q[logπθ(a∣st)+βlogτ¯(at−1,a∣x)]+ℋ(q)+const.-\mathrm{KL}(q\|r)=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim q}\big[\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s_{t})+\beta\log\bar{\tau}(a_{t-1},a\mid x)\big]+\mathcal{H}(q)+\text{const}. (21)

For η=1\eta=1, maximizing Eq. (15) is equivalent, up to constants, to the KL projection

minqKL(q∥1Zexp(logπθ(⋅∣st)+βlogτ¯(at−1,⋅∣x))),\min_{q}\ \mathrm{KL}\!\left(q\,\middle\|\,\tfrac{1}{Z}\exp\!\big(\log\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t})+\beta\log\bar{\tau}(a_{t-1},\cdot\mid x)\big)\right), (22)

where ZZ is the normalizer over 𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t}. This view clarifies the role of pheromone as an explicit transition prior in log space: actions must be supported by the neural policy and by the accumulated transition statistics encoded in τ¯\bar{\tau}, which increases the probability of historically successful tool-transition edges under the current task context.

Appendix B B: Algorithm Implementation Details and Training Mechanisms

Base model adaptation

We instantiate PhGPO on instruction-tuned backbones used in our main experiments, including Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3.1-8B. We apply LoRA for parameter-efficient adaptation by freezing backbone weights and inserting low-rank adapters with rank r=64r{=}64 and scaling α=128\alpha{=}128 into standard projection modules. All stages use the tokenizer and chat template of the corresponding backbone, and tool planning is trained as a generative decision process over the same two-layer action space described in Sec. Tool-Transition Graph from MCP. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/PhGPO-Pheromone-Guided-Policy-Optimization-for-Long-Horizon-Tool-Planning-CB1C.

Progressive training pipeline

Training follows the progressive pipeline described in Sec. Pheromone-Guided Policy Optimization Training. It begins with supervised warm-up using the next-tool prediction objective in Eq. (6), which provides a stable initialization for tool selection. After warm-up, training uses a progressive schedule that mixes oracle guidance with pheromone-guided sampling. At each decision step, the agent takes the reference action with probability ptfp_{\text{tf}}; otherwise it samples actions from the pheromone-guided distribution in Eq. (7), as specified in Eq. (9). Policy updates use the mixed objective in Eq. (10), where λ\lambda is annealed downward to shift learning from imitation toward policy optimization. In parallel, a horizon curriculum increases the rollout horizon from shorter to longer trajectories. We also schedule β\beta in Eq. (7) and ww in Eq. (5) upward as more verified trajectories are accumulated, which increases the influence of the explicit transition prior and task-dependent evidence. When ptfp_{\text{tf}} approaches zero and λ\lambda becomes small, rollouts become fully policy-driven under pheromone guidance, and optimization follows the policy objective described in Sec. Pheromone-Guided Policy Optimization Training. For group-based learning, we use M=5M{=}5 rollouts per instance, consistent with Sec. Experiment Setup.

Mixed training objective under teacher forcing

During progressive training pipeline, rollouts are generated under a mixed behavior rule that combines oracle actions and pheromone-guided sampling. Let at∗a_{t}^{\ast} denote the reference action provided by the benchmark instance, and let π~\tilde{\pi} denote the pheromone-guided sampling distribution in Eq. (7). The behavior distribution used for rollout generation is

πmix​(at∣st)=ptf⋅δ⁡(at=at∗)+(1−ptf)⋅π~​(at∣st),\pi_{\text{mix}}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})=p_{\text{tf}}\cdot\delta(a_{t}=a_{t}^{\ast})\;+\;(1-p_{\text{tf}})\cdot\tilde{\pi}(a_{t}\mid s_{t}), (23)

where δ⁡(⋅)\delta(\cdot) is a point mass on the oracle action. We record the executed action ata_{t} at every step, together with its log-probability under the current policy at rollout time, log⁡πθold​(at∣st)\log\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_{t}\mid s_{t}).

Policy optimization uses GRPO with a PPO-style clipped surrogate. For each training instance, we sample a group of MM tool-use trajectories and compute their returns {Rm}m=1M\{R_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M} (Sec. B). We normalize returns within the group to obtain advantages AmA_{m} as in Eq. (8). The policy-gradient loss is computed on executed actions under πmix\pi_{\text{mix}}:

ℒPG=−𝔼m,t​[min⁡(rm,t​(θ)​Am,clip⁡(rm,t​(θ),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)​Am)],rm,t​(θ)=πθ​(am,t∣sm,t)πθold​(am,t∣sm,t).\mathcal{L}_{\text{PG}}=-\mathbb{E}_{m,t}\!\left[\min\!\Bigl(r_{m,t}(\theta)A_{m},\;\mathrm{clip}(r_{m,t}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)A_{m}\Bigr)\right],\qquad r_{m,t}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a_{m,t}\mid s_{m,t})}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_{m,t}\mid s_{m,t})}. (24)

When an action is oracle-selected, Eq. (24) still evaluates its probability under πθ\pi_{\theta}, since that action is the one executed in the environment under πmix\pi_{\text{mix}}. In parallel, the supervised term in Eq. (10) is computed as a next-action cross-entropy against at∗a_{t}^{\ast}. As ptfp_{\text{tf}} is annealed toward zero, the rollout distribution approaches fully policy-driven pheromone-guided sampling, and updates become dominated by autonomous decisions.

Pheromone and memory

PhGPO maintains pheromone on two types of edges: tool-transition edges (vi,vj)∈ℰ(v_{i},v_{j})\in\mathcal{E} and tool-to-invocation edges (vi,vi(k))∈ℰarg(v_{i},v_{i}^{(k)})\in\mathcal{E}_{\text{arg}} defined in Sec. Tool-Transition Graph from MCP. We maintain task-agnostic pheromones τToolagn\tau^{\text{agn}}_{\text{Tool}} and τArgagn\tau^{\text{agn}}_{\text{Arg}}, and we clip pheromone values to [τmin,τmax][\tau_{\min},\tau_{\max}] as described in Sec. Pheromone as an Explicit Transition Prior.

Task embeddings and sentence encoder.

Task-dependent pheromones use a fixed sentence encoder ϕ\phi to embed the task text xx into a dense vector 𝒆=ϕ⁡(x)\bm{e}=\phi(x). In our reference implementation, ϕ\phi is instantiated with SentenceTransformer(all-MiniLM-L6-v2). Edge memory banks store tuples (𝒆,q)(\bm{e},q) for each edge, where qq is the quality score of the corresponding tool-use trajectory (Sec. B).

We additionally maintain edge-indexed memory banks for task-dependent pheromones. For a tool-transition edge (vi,vj)(v_{i},v_{j}), its memory bank ℳi​j\mathcal{M}_{ij} stores tuples (𝒆,q)(\bm{e},q), where 𝒆=ϕ⁡(x)\bm{e}{=}\phi(x) is the task embedding and qq is the quality score associated with a verified tool-use trajectory that contains this edge. Given a task xx, we compute task-dependent pheromones by retrieval and similarity-weighted aggregation as in Eq. (3), estimate confidence by Eq. (4), and then combine task-agnostic and task-dependent pheromones using Eq. (5). We apply the same mechanism to tool-to-invocation edges for τArg\tau_{\text{Arg}}.

Rationale and locality of the confidence score.

The confidence score in Eq. (4) is computed locally from the retrieved set ℳi​j​(x)\mathcal{M}_{ij}(x) for the queried task xx. In particular, nactn_{\text{act}} counts the number of retrieved memories that pass activation thresholds, smaxs_{\max} is the maximum similarity among activated memories, and q¯\bar{q} is the mean quality score over the same activated subset. We incorporate q¯\bar{q} in confidence to gate task-dependent pheromones when retrieval returns semantically similar but consistently low-quality memories. This design keeps the fused explicit transition prior conservative, assigning higher weight to context-aware pheromones only when retrieved evidence is both relevant (high similarity) and reliable (high average quality), and otherwise falling back to task-agnostic pheromones.

Reward signals and trajectory quality score

We distinguish two quantities computed per rollout: the episode return RR used for policy optimization, and the trajectory quality score q⁡(ξ)q(\xi) used for pheromone deposition and memory writing. They are computed together during rollout generation but serve different roles in training.

Reward structure and episode return.

For each rollout, we compute an episode return RR as the sum of step-level rewards and an outcome-level bonus. At each step tt, the step reward decomposes into an intent component and an execution component,

rt=rtintent+rtexec.r_{t}=r_{t}^{\text{intent}}+r_{t}^{\text{exec}}. (25)

The intent reward rtintentr_{t}^{\text{intent}} encourages selecting the correct next base tool. Concretely, we assign +0.5+0.5 for an exact match to the reference next base tool, and +0.2+0.2 for a category-consistent selection (i.e., the predicted tool belongs to the same predefined tool category as the reference). To mitigate error propagation, we additionally provide a recovery bonus of +0.1+0.1 when the previous step is incorrect but the current step returns to the reference tool.11 1 This recovery term is only applied when at−1≠at−1∗a_{t-1}\neq a^{*}_{t-1} and at=at∗a_{t}=a^{*}_{t}. Otherwise, rtintent=0r_{t}^{\text{intent}}=0. The execution reward rtexecr_{t}^{\text{exec}} is assigned after simulating the selected tool invocation (Sec. B). We assign +0.5+0.5 when the simulator returns a valid execution without triggering an error pattern, and −0.5-0.5 when an execution error or timeout is detected. We treat invalid argument formatting as an execution failure and apply the same penalty.

After the rollout terminates, we add an outcome-level bonus that rewards completed episodes and, when completion is not achieved, provides graded bonuses based on the final Match Ratio. The episode return used by GRPO is

R=∑t=1Trt+routcome.R=\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{t}\;+\;r_{\text{outcome}}. (26)

Trajectory quality score for pheromone updates.

The pheromone deposition mechanism in Eq. (1) relies on a trajectory quality score q⁡(ξ)∈[0,1]q(\xi)\in[0,1]. In our benchmark setting, each instance provides a reference tool-use trajectory ξ∗=(a1∗,…,aT∗)\xi^{\ast}=(a_{1}^{\ast},\dots,a_{T}^{\ast}). Given a rollout trajectory ξ=(a1,…,aT)\xi=(a_{1},\dots,a_{T}), we define

q(ξ)=Match(ξ,ξ∗)=1T∑t=1T𝕀[tool(at)=tool(at∗)],q(\xi)\;=\;\mathrm{Match}(\xi,\xi^{\ast})\;=\;\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{I}\!\left[\mathrm{tool}(a_{t})=\mathrm{tool}(a_{t}^{\ast})\right], (27)

where tool⁡(⋅)\mathrm{tool}(\cdot) extracts the base tool identity from the two-layer action, and the indicator compares step-aligned tool identities. This definition uses the reference tool-use trajectory, and it is computed independently from the environmental return RR in Eq. (26). We maintain both quantities since RR provides the learning signal for policy optimization, while q⁡(ξ)q(\xi) provides a stable and interpretable score for updating the explicit transition prior.

Teacher forcing and model-driven quality.

During mixed rollouts with oracle guidance, we record a per-step teacher-forcing mask indicating whether ata_{t} was oracle-selected. We additionally report a model-driven Match Ratio computed on the subset of steps not teacher-forced:

qmodel(ξ)=1|𝒯model|∑t∈𝒯model𝕀[tool(at)=tool(at∗)],𝒯model={t:at is not oracle-selected}.q_{\text{model}}(\xi)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{\text{model}}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{\text{model}}}\mathbb{I}\!\left[\mathrm{tool}(a_{t})=\mathrm{tool}(a_{t}^{\ast})\right],\qquad\mathcal{T}_{\text{model}}=\{t:\;a_{t}\text{ is not oracle-selected}\}. (28)

This quantity diagnoses how much alignment is attributable to autonomous decisions. In addition, we only collect elite replay trajectories after ptfp_{\text{tf}} decays below a threshold, which limits the impact of heavily teacher-forced trajectories on subsequent pheromone reinforcement.

Tool execution simulation

Our training environment executes tool calls through a simulator, not by invoking external APIs. This design keeps rollouts reproducible, avoids network variability, and prevents unintended side effects. Given the selected tool and its argument invocation, the simulator produces a tool output and a completion signal that indicates whether the episode has reached a terminal success state. The simulator can replay cached outputs from an offline database, and it also supports a pluggable LLM-based simulator backend that generates tool outputs via an OpenAI-compatible interface. The execution reward in Sec. B is computed from this simulated output, assigning positive reward to valid executions and penalizing execution errors or malformed outputs.

Fairness of comparisons.

To ensure fair comparisons, all methods share the same backbones, tool set, decoding configuration, rollout horizon limits, and evaluation protocol, and they are trained under the same computational budget whenever applicable. For baseline methods that require tool-format awareness (e.g., producing valid tool names or argument fields), we apply the same lightweight tool-format fine-tuning procedure used in our approach (e.g., the same LoRA setup on identical tool-call supervision) to calibrate tool syntax and reduce avoidable execution failures. This control isolates the effect of the learning algorithm and sampling strategy, and it prevents differences in tool-call formatting from dominating the reported performance.

Appendix C C: Datasets

We evaluate on three long-horizon tool-use benchmarks: Toolathlon, TRAJECT-Bench, and TOUCAN. Each benchmark provides (i) executable tools or tool interfaces, and (ii) a reference tool-use sequence, which enables fine-grained comparison between predicted tool-use sequences and the reference. Following our main experimental protocol, we use the official splits when available, and we only keep episodes whose reference tool-use sequences are verifiably successful.

To align with our Tool-Transition Graph action space (Sec. Tool-Transition Graph from MCP), we report dataset-scale statistics in terms of: L1 Tools, the number of base tools in 𝒱Tool\mathcal{V}_{\text{Tool}}; L2 Tools, the number of argument-invocation patterns aggregated across tools in 𝒱Arg\mathcal{V}_{\text{Arg}}; and Avg Steps, the average number of tool calls per verifiably successful reference tool-use sequence in the retained episodes.

Toolathlon.

Toolathlon is a long-horizon benchmark designed for realistic, execution-based evaluation across diverse software applications. After mapping tool calls into our Tool-Transition Graph action representation, Toolathlon contains 618 L1 tools and 1,250 L2 argument-invocation patterns. Among the retained verifiably successful reference sequences, the average tool-call length is 13.48 steps.

TRAJECT-Bench.

TRAJECT-Bench is a trajectory-aware benchmark that emphasizes correctness of tool selection, tool arguments, and dependency or ordering constraints along the full tool-use trajectory. In our Tool-Transition Graph representation, TRAJECT-Bench contains 381 L1 tools and 715 L2 argument-invocation patterns. Among the retained verifiably successful reference sequences, the average tool-call length is 6.36 steps.

TOUCAN (Multi-step only).

TOUCAN is a large-scale tool-agent dataset synthesized from real-world Model Context Protocol (MCP) environments. We only consider the Multi-step subset, defined as instances with at least two tool calls in the reference sequence. In our Tool-Transition Graph representation, the Multi-step subset contains 850 L1 tools and 15,294 L2 argument-invocation patterns. Among the retained verifiably successful reference sequences, the average tool-call length is 3.16 steps.

Appendix D D: Ablation Study on Pheromone Influence Parameter β\beta

This appendix studies the pheromone influence parameter β\beta in Eq. (7), which scales the explicit transition prior during pheromone-guided sampling. β\beta controls how strongly historically verified tool-transition patterns bias the next tool choice, shaping the exploration exploitation trade-off in long-horizon planning.

Specifically, we sample tools from

p⁡(at∣st,at−1)∝exp⁡(log⁡πθ​(at∣st)+β​log⁡τTool​(at−1,at∣x)),p(a_{t}\mid s_{t},a_{t-1})\propto\exp\!\Big(\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})+\beta\log\tau_{\text{Tool}}(a_{t-1},a_{t}\mid x)\Big), (29)

where β≥0\beta\geq 0 determines the strength of pheromone guidance. β=0\beta=0 removes pheromone, while larger β\beta increasingly favors transitions with higher pheromone, which can reduce exploration if set too aggressively.

Experimental Setup

We ablate β\beta on Toolathlon with Qwen2.5-7B. We compare: (i) β=0\beta=0 (no pheromone), (ii) β=1\beta=1 (fixed moderate), (iii) β=5\beta=5 (strong over-guidance), and (iv) our dynamic schedule, where β\beta is linearly increased from 00 to 0.80.8 over the first 30% of epochs and then kept at 0.80.8. All variants share the same backbone, optimizer, learning rate schedule, rollout group size (M=5M=5), and evaluation protocol. We train for 25 epochs and report Match Ratio (Match R.) and Next-tool Accuracy (TAcc). We also measure Exploration Diversity as the normalized entropy of the action distribution over tools:

Diversity=H⁡(π)log⁡|A|∈[0,1].\text{Diversity}=\frac{H(\pi)}{\log|A|}\in[0,1]. (30)

Results

Table 4 shows that pheromone guidance improves performance over β=0\beta=0, while excessive guidance (β=5\beta=5) harms both Match R. and TAcc. Our dynamic schedule achieves the best results, indicating that gradually increasing pheromone influence matches the increasing reliability of accumulated pheromone statistics.

Interpretation.

With β=0\beta=0, the policy remains highly diverse but learns slowly, suggesting unfocused exploration. With β=5\beta=5, the policy becomes nearly deterministic and underperforms, consistent with premature over-exploitation of early transition patterns. Fixed β=1\beta=1 provides a stable improvement over β=0\beta=0, but it cannot adapt to the evolving quality of pheromone statistics. Dynamic β\beta preserves early diversity for discovery and then reduces diversity to a stable mid-range as training progresses, aligning improved Match R. with higher TAcc. Variance in the diversity curve is expected because it is estimated from a small number of rollouts per epoch (M=5M=5), while Match R. and TAcc average across trajectories and evaluation instances.

Pheromone guidance benefits long-horizon tool planning, but its strength must be calibrated. Extreme settings either remove reusable transition information (β=0\beta=0) or suppress exploration (β=5\beta=5). A progressive schedule for β\beta yields the best balance, improving both sequence-level Match R. and step-level TAcc.

Appendix E E: Training Dynamics and Pheromone Evolution

Training dynamics. To assess optimization stability, we visualize the evolution of policy performance together with the evolution of the pheromone structure in Figure 5. We report the average return measured over training rollouts for each backbone. Figure 5(a) shows a consistent upward trend across all four backbone models, indicating that PhGPO steadily improves the rollout-level objective. The smallest backbone, Qwen2.5-1.5B, reaches competitive returns compared with larger models, which suggests that the reusable tool-transition patterns reduces the difficulty of long-horizon exploration for lower-capacity policies. The curves exhibit sustained improvement without abrupt collapses, which is consistent with stable optimization under our training configuration.

Pheromone graph growth. Figure 5(b) tracks the growth of the pheromone graph, measured by the number of discovered edges that receive pheromone statistics. These edges correspond to tool-transition edges, and they can also include argument-invocation edges when tool invocations are represented at the argument level. We observe rapid edge discovery during early epochs, followed by a clear saturation. This trend indicates that the agent quickly identifies a broad set of feasible tool transitions and then concentrates updates on a more stable subset. Under pheromone evaporation, older statistics gradually lose influence, which keeps the explicit transition prior responsive to recent verified tool-use trajectories while preventing unbounded accumulation.

Relationship between returns and pheromone. The increase in average return coincides with the period where the pheromone graph expands and then stabilizes. This alignment suggests that improving performance is accompanied by accumulating transition evidence on the pheromone graph. Once most frequently used transitions have been identified, performance improvements continue primarily through adjusting the relative strengths of already discovered edges and improving the policy probabilities on those transitions.

Appendix F F: Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis

This appendix reports a sensitivity analysis of eight key hyperparameters in PhGPO on Toolathlon. We vary one hyperparameter at a time while keeping all others fixed to the default values in Table 5. We train with Qwen2.5-7B and report Match Ratio on the test set. Each configuration is evaluated with 3 random seeds, and Figure 6 shows the mean with ±1\pm 1 standard deviation. Red stars and dashed lines indicate our chosen values.

Hyperparameters. We group the parameters into pheromone guidance and policy optimization. Pheromone guidance includes the pheromone influence β\beta Eq. (7), evaporation rate ρ\rho and deposition rate α\alpha Eq. (1), and the context weight ww Eq. (5). Policy optimization includes GRPO group size MM, RL fine-tuning learning rate η\eta, final teacher forcing probability ptfp_{\mathrm{tf}}, and entropy regularization coefficient γ\gamma.

Overall observations. Figure 6 shows that our defaults fall within, or very close to, the best-performing regions across all eight parameters. Among pheromone parameters, β\beta and ρ\rho are the most sensitive: under-guidance with small β\beta reduces the benefit of the explicit transition prior, while overly large β\beta can suppress exploration. ρ\rho exhibits a narrow optimum around 0.010.01, where older statistics decay slowly enough to remain useful but not so slowly that early transitions dominate indefinitely. In contrast, α\alpha is comparatively robust, with a broad near-optimal region around 1.01.0. The context weight ww peaks around 0.50.5, indicating that combining task-dependent and task-agnostic pheromone improves performance, while extreme values over-emphasize one source.

For optimization parameters, MM shows diminishing returns: performance improves rapidly from M=1M=1 and saturates around M=5M=5. The RL learning rate η\eta exhibits a narrow optimum on a log scale, consistent with conservative fine-tuning requirements in the final stage. The final teacher forcing probability ptfp_{\mathrm{tf}} follows a U-shaped pattern, where too little oracle guidance destabilizes early learning and pheromone initialization, and too much oracle guidance limits autonomous improvement. The entropy coefficient γ\gamma has a broad plateau around 0.0050.005, maintaining sufficient exploration without preventing convergence.

Experimental Guide. When adapting PhGPO, tuning ρ\rho and β\beta is most important due to their sharper sensitivity. The remaining parameters admit wider plateaus, and our defaults provide a strong starting point. Progressive schedules for β\beta, ww, and ptfp_{\mathrm{tf}} are consistent with these curves because they avoid committing to aggressive guidance before the corresponding statistics become reliable.

Appendix G G: Generality Across Policy Optimization Backbones

This appendix shows that PhGPO is not tied to a specific policy optimization backbone. PhGPO defines (i) pheromone as an explicit transition prior on tool-transition edges and tool-to-invocation edges (Sec. Pheromone as an Explicit Transition Prior), (ii) pheromone-guided sampling during rollout generation (Eq. (7)), and (iii) pheromone updates via deposition and evaporation (Eq. (1) and Eq. (5)). These components are independent of the choice of the policy-gradient optimizer used to update πθ\pi_{\theta}. In practice, we can replace GRPO with other on-policy optimizers, while keeping the same pheromone-guided rollout distribution and pheromone bookkeeping.

GRPO, PPO, and RLOO backbones

We describe three interchangeable optimization backbones under the same rollout protocol. For each task instance, we sample MM tool-use trajectories from the pheromone-guided distribution in Eq. (7), obtain sequence-level returns {Rm}m=1M\{R_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M}, and update the policy using a clipped policy-gradient objective. Across all three backbones, pheromone-guided sampling and pheromone updates remain unchanged.

GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). GRPO uses group-relative normalization to construct a sequence-level advantage for each rollout:

Am=Rm−R¯σR+ϵ,R¯=1M​∑m=1MRm,A_{m}=\frac{R_{m}-\bar{R}}{\sigma_{R}+\epsilon},\qquad\bar{R}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}R_{m}, (31)

and applies a PPO-style clipped ratio objective with AmA_{m} (Sec. Pheromone-Guided Policy Optimization Training). This backbone does not require an explicit value function and leverages within-group contrasts.

PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization). PPO constructs an advantage using a baseline b⁡(⋅)b(\cdot), which can be implemented as a learned value head or a running baseline. In our setting, we use a sequence-level advantage

Am=Rm−b⁡(x),A_{m}=R_{m}-b(x), (32)

and optimize the standard clipped surrogate objective:

ℒPPO=−𝔼⁡[min⁡(rt​(θ)​Am,clip⁡(rt​(θ),1−ε,1+ε)​Am)],\mathcal{L}^{\text{PPO}}=-\mathbb{E}\Big[\min\big(r_{t}(\theta)A_{m},\ \mathrm{clip}(r_{t}(\theta),1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)A_{m}\big)\Big], (33)

where rt​(θ)=πθ​(at∣st)/πθold​(at∣st)r_{t}(\theta)=\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})/\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_{t}\mid s_{t}) is the probability ratio at tool-decision steps.

RLOO (Leave-one-out baseline). RLOO avoids learning a value function and uses a leave-one-out baseline computed from the other rollouts in the same group:

b−m=1M−1​∑j≠mRj,Am=Rm−b−m.b_{-m}=\frac{1}{M-1}\sum_{j\neq m}R_{j},\qquad A_{m}=R_{m}-b_{-m}. (34)

The policy is then updated using the same clipped objective as Eq. (33), with AmA_{m} replaced by the leave-one-out advantage.

Experimental protocol on Toolathlon

We evaluate optimizer-agnosticity on Toolathlon using Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3.1-8B. All runs use the same action space, pheromone-guided sampling rule (Eq. (7)), pheromone update rule (Eq. (1)), and the same progressive pipeline in Sec. Pheromone-Guided Policy Optimization Training. The only change is the policy optimization backbone used to update πθ\pi_{\theta}. We report sequence-level Match Ratio (Match R., %) and Next-tool Accuracy (TAcc, %).

Appendix H H: Extended Visualization on Longer Tool-use Trajectories

This appendix provides an extended visualization showing that the pheromone-based explicit transition prior remains informative on longer tool-use trajectories. For readability, we visualize a 10-tool subset of the tool-transition space, while the underlying episode involves a longer reference tool-use trajectory in the same MCP execution environment. All visualizations report the fused tool-transition pheromone τTool(⋅∣x)\tau_{\text{Tool}}(\cdot\mid x) defined in Eq. (5), where task-dependent evidence is retrieved by Eq. (3) and confidence is computed by Eq. (4). Pheromone updates follow deposition and evaporation in Eq. (1).

10-tool subset visualization

Figure 7 visualizes pheromone evolution on a representative long-horizon instance using the following 10 tools:

QueryWandB →\rightarrow WriteFile →\rightarrow ReadFile →\rightarrow PyExecute →\rightarrow WriteFile →\rightarrow ReadFile →\rightarrow RunCmd →\rightarrow ListDir →\rightarrow ReadFile →\rightarrow ClaimDone

The heatmaps (top row) show the fused pheromone matrix restricted to these tools at several training checkpoints. Reference-chain transitions that appear in this instance are highlighted in red. As training proceeds, pheromone mass becomes increasingly concentrated on the reference-chain transitions within this 10-tool subset, while many off-chain transitions fade as evaporation reduces the influence of older or weakly supported statistics. This pattern indicates that the explicit transition prior becomes more selective over time, amplifying transitions that recur in verified successful tool-use trajectories.

The bar plot (bottom row) reports pheromone values along the reference-chain transitions within the same 10-tool subset at the corresponding checkpoints. Earlier transitions often exhibit stronger reinforcement because they are visited more frequently across verified successful trajectories and because early tool choices constrain later reachable states in long tool-use trajectories. Later transitions remain distinguishable from the background, which indicates that the pheromone signal is not limited to prefix segments and can provide guidance throughout the chain.

Appendix I I: Time Efficiency: Path Discovery Speed

This appendix provides a qualitative analysis of training-time efficiency. We compare PhGPO against an ablation that removes the pheromone prior, and examine how quickly each method discovers the first high-quality tool-use trajectory on Toolathlon episodes. A trajectory is considered high-quality when its match quality satisfies q⁡(ξ)≥0.6q(\xi)\geq 0.6.

Experimental protocol We evaluate two configurations on Toolathlon with Qwen2.5-7B:

  • •

    PhGPO (Full): rollouts are sampled from the fused distribution that incorporates pheromone as an explicit transition prior (Eq. (7)), with the progressive schedule described in Sec. Pheromone-Guided Policy Optimization Training.

  • •

    GRPO w/o pheromone: we set β=0\beta=0 throughout training, removing pheromone guidance during rollout generation while keeping the remaining pipeline identical (same curriculum, the same oracle-mixing rule via ptfp_{\text{tf}}, and the same mixed objective).

For each Toolathlon episode, we record the earliest training step at which at least one generated trajectory reaches q⁡(ξ)≥0.6q(\xi)\geq 0.6, and summarize the trend across episodes and trajectory-length bins.

Results. Figure 8 summarizes the path discovery speed measured by the first occurrence of a high-quality trajectory (q⁡(ξ)≥0.6q(\xi)\geq 0.6). In panel (a), PhGPO maintains a higher high-quality match rate than the ablation without pheromone at matched training steps, and it reaches the same coverage level with fewer training steps. The gap remains visible across the training range shown in the figure, indicating more efficient discovery of high-quality trajectories under the same budget. Panel (b) reports the relative speedup across trajectory-length bins. The speedup stays positive across bins and varies within a narrow range, and the fitted linear trend is close to flat. This pattern suggests that the efficiency gain is not restricted to a specific horizon, and it remains broadly stable as the average trajectory length increases.

Interpretation The trend is consistent with the role of pheromone as an explicit transition prior during trajectory generation. Without pheromone (β=0\beta=0), rollout groups sampled only from the policy can be dominated by uniformly low-quality trajectories in a large tool space, which weakens group-relative learning signals. With pheromone guidance, historically verified tool-transition edges receive higher sampling probability, which reduces wasted exploration on low-potential transitions and increases the likelihood that each rollout group contains informative contrasts for group-based policy optimization. This mechanism can benefit from partial matches: any trajectory that reaches q⁡(ξ)≥0.6q(\xi)\geq 0.6 can contribute transition statistics, even when it is not an exact match to the reference.

Implications These results indicate that PhGPO not only improves final performance, but also improves training-time efficiency by accelerating the discovery of high-quality tool-use trajectories. This property is particularly relevant in execution-based environments where tool calls are costly.

Appendix J J: Simulated Tool Execution

Our training and evaluation use a simulated tool environment. Tool calls are not executed against real external APIs or services. Instead, each tool invocation is routed to a tool-output simulator that returns a plausible response conditioned on the current context. This design provides a controlled and reproducible feedback channel for learning tool-use trajectories, while avoiding external side effects and service availability issues.

LLM-based tool-output simulator

We implement an LLM-based simulator that generates tool outputs from structured context. Given a tool variant name, its arguments, the task name, the user request, and a truncated history of recent tool interactions, the simulator constructs a prompt that includes: (i) the task and user request, (ii) the recent tool-call history (with any completion markers removed), (iii) the current tool name, its original tool name, and its natural-language description, (iv) the provided arguments (or expected keys when arguments are absent). The simulator then queries an instruction-following model to produce a short response that resembles a real tool return value (for example, a JSON snippet, a status string, or a concise result summary).

In our experiments, we use qwen3-235b-a22b-thinking-2507 as the simulator model through an OpenAI-compatible chat-completions endpoint. We fix the simulator system prompt to enforce output-only behavior, and we strip common explanatory prefixes and markdown formatting during post-processing to keep outputs consistent with a tool API style.

Completion detection via an explicit marker

The simulator also provides a lightweight termination signal. After generating a tool output, the simulator decides whether the current interaction history already completes the user request. If it judges the task complete, it appends a dedicated marker <<END>> on a separate final line. We remove this marker from the returned tool output and store the completion flag separately. This enables consistent stopping behavior during rollout generation without requiring an additional model call.

Caching and fallback behavior

To reduce simulator calls and stabilize training, we cache simulator outputs using a content hash over the tool variant, task name, user request, truncated history, and arguments. When the LLM simulator is unavailable or fails, we optionally fall back to a pool-based simulator that samples from pre-defined outputs, and we use a simple default template as a final fallback. These mechanisms preserve the tool-use interface while keeping the environment feedback stable under large-scale training.
